# ADR 0005 — A comment says what the caller must know and why the code is so, decided per place in the source

> **In short.** In the context of a codebase that Claude sessions will write and read again in every session,
> facing comments that grow into history, repeat the code and cost context on every read, we decided for one rule
> per place in the source, saying what a comment there carries, plus prohibitions that apply everywhere, all held by
> a comment gate, and against a single length limit or no rule at all, to keep function contracts at the code and
> history in git, accepting that a few points depend on a judgment the gate can only report as a candidate.

## Context and problem

Pixecutive has no code yet; the first files are the scripts, hooks and gates of its own setup. Every file will be
read by Claude sessions again and again, so each comment line is paid for on every read. A comment that tells how
the code came to be goes stale and is never corrected; `git blame` holds the same information and does not lie.

What a comment should carry depends on where it stands: above an export, inside a body, at the head of a file, in a
test. A single length limit cannot tell a short contract from a short repetition of the code.

## Decision drivers

- A function contract that exists nowhere else must survive.
- History belongs to git, decisions to ADRs, not to the source.
- What a tool can read (JSDoc tags, a generated-file header) is worth more than the same statement as free text.
- Each rule must be checkable, or it becomes the next prose that is read and broken.

## Considered options

- **A — One rule per place**, plus prohibitions that apply everywhere, held by a gate.
- **B — One length limit for every comment.**
- **C — No rule; judge in review.**

## Decision

Chosen: **A**, because the place decides whether a comment is justified better than its length does.

**Where a comment must stand**

1. **Every exported function, method and component carries a JSDoc block:** what it does and what the caller must
   know, not why it was built this way. `[Gate check-comments]`
2. **A type gets a block when its name does not carry its meaning**: unit, range, invariant.
   `[Gate check-comments reports candidates · Agent adversarial-review judges]`
3. **A comment inside a body explains business logic, in at most three lines.** `[Gate check-comments]`
4. **A file head stands only when the name does not say the purpose, in at most three lines.** For scripts, hooks
   and gates it is required and says what they reject. `[Gate check-comments]`

**What never stands in a comment**

5. **No history:** no date, no "previously", no quote. `[Gate check-comments]`
6. **A ticket number only at a TODO or a deliberate exception**, never as a trace of an ordinary decision.
   `[Gate check-comments]`
7. **No comment that repeats the code, no commented-out code, no section banner, no apology.**
   `[Gate check-comments]`

**The other places**

8. **No end-of-line comments.** `[Gate check-comments]`
9. **No comments in JSX.** A part that needs explaining gets a name of its own. `[Gate check-comments]`
10. **Tests follow the same rules.** `[Gate check-comments]`
11. **`eslint-disable` and `@ts-expect-error` carry their reason.** `[Gate check-comments · Planned PIX-7: Lint]`
12. **A TODO needs a ticket; FIXME, HACK and XXX are forbidden.** `[Gate check-comments]`
13. **A generated file says who generated it.** `[Gate check-comments · Gate check-generated]`

**The form**

14. **`@param` and `@returns` only where the signature does not tell; `@throws` always when a function throws.**
    No signature shows what is thrown. `[Gate check-comments]`

The rule set is run on every write by `quality-guard` and on the staged state by pre-commit; the `comment-audit`
skill runs the same rule set over existing files and never holds a second copy of it.
`[Hook quality-guard · Hook pre-commit · Skill comment-audit]`

### Consequences

- Good, because history stays in git and the source carries only what is true now.
- Good, because a thrown error is always documented, while `@param` lines that repeat the type are never written.
- Good, because every hook and gate states in its first lines what it rejects.
- Bad, because points 2 and 3 and the exception in point 6 rest on a judgment; the gate reports candidates and the
  review before the pull request decides.
- Not decided here: how controllers document their routes. That depends on the server framework, which is not
  chosen yet.

### Confirmation

`check-comments` has a probe per rule that plants one violation (a date, a quote, a banner, a commented-out
statement, an end-of-line comment, a TODO without ticket, a FIXME, an undocumented export, a throwing function
without `@throws`, a hook without head) and turns red on it, then green on the fixed file. The probe is registered in
`.claude/data/precommit-checks.tsv`. See [ADR 0008](0008-testing-and-gates.md) for why every gate needs one.

## Mechanics

No diagram. The decision is a list of rules per place, each with its check; there is no branch to draw.

## Rejected

- **B — one length limit for everything.** Hits a long contract and a short repetition alike.
- **C — no rule, judged in review.** Every review judges differently, and nothing turns red.
- **`@param` and `@returns` on every function.** Adds lines that repeat the signature.
- **Comments that record history.** They go stale; git already holds the history.
